name: Public Procurement
description: Uncover the hidden patterns in public procurement. Our primary indicators reveal critical insights into procurement transparency. Explore contract modifications, instances where no call for tenders was published, non-open procedures, single bidding cases, tax haven connections, and beneficiary ownership transparency. These experience-based indicators provide actionable intelligence for reformers.
methodology:
Our public procurement integrity methodology uses a systemic approach to identify patterns (easy red flags) in public procurement that may be signs of corruption and other types of illicit behavior. We use a small number the five set of widely available indicators to identify integrity risks at key stages of the procurement process. 

 

Remember: high risk values may not necessarily be evidence of corruption and could be influenced by underlying market structures. Regardless of whether a risk is an indicator of actual corruption, monitoring atypical procurement practices can help to identify and address underlying inefficiencies in the procurement system. 

 The numerical value of an integrity indicator represents the number of risky contracts as a percentage of all measurable contracts for a given country or market. For example, if 30 contracts in a cohort of 100 were awarded using non-open procedures, the indicator value will be 0.3. Countries are also assigned an indicator risk level based on its position relative to other countries (high, medium, or low). 

Within a country, the contracts can be analyzed by product market, contract value, year and sub-national regions, where data is available. 

Other important variables such as the transparency, size and value of procurement can be measured using the data availability dashboards.  

 

The data was collected by the Government Transparency Institute (GTI) for UNDP’s Global Initiative on Measuring Corruption,  from the publicly available data of national government procurement systems, then processed to create standardized, comparable datasets that enable analysis across countries and time. 
 
The full methodology can be downloaded from the resources section of this website.

name: World Bank's Enterprise Survey
description: What do businesses really experience on the ground? Go beyond perception to understand real encounters with corruption. Our indicators capture the incidence of corrupt practices, document specific practices businesses encounter, and reveal counter measures organizations implement. This ground-truth data empowers evidence-based strategies.
methodology:
The World Bank Enterprise Surveys (WBES) provide firm-level data on the business environment and its interaction with enterprise performance. They are implemented by the World Bank, usually through local partners, following a harmonised global methodology that ensures results are comparable across countries and over time.
The surveys cover the formal private sector only, excluding the informal economy, agriculture, extractive industries, and public sector organisations including also public enterprises. The target population consists of registered business establishments with at least five employees. Samples are drawn through stratified random selection, with strata defined by firm size, main activity, and region. The respondent for the WBES is a top-level decision maker (owner, director, etc.) of the establishment sampled. 
The WBES questionnaire is standardised across all participating countries and consists mainly of factual items answered by the owner or top manager of the business establishment. It covers more than a dozen thematic areas—such as access to finance, infrastructure, trade, regulation, innovation, and labour practices—also including questions on corruption. Around ninety percent of questions are factual, while a small subset captures perceptions. Interviews are conducted face-to-face, most recently through computer-assisted personal interviewing (CAPI). Corruption-related questions of the WBES clarify bribery pressure as experienced by sampled business establishments in various contexts (taxation, procurement, permits/licences and access to utility services), and include an assessment of how much of a burden is corruption in the particular economy for the business establishment interviewed.  
Data is collected through in-person interviewing, implementing rigorous controls through extensive field supervision, back-checks, and internal validation by the World Bank team. 
All microdata, questionnaires, and methodological notes are publicly available at https://www.enterprisesurveys.org
